subject: mathematics
title: Understand area and perimeter
promise: This starts from what area and perimeter actually ARE — the space inside a shape, and the distance around it — before any formula. Get those two pictures clear and the formulas stop being things to memorise and become things that are obvious.

sections.heading: Area is the space inside
sections.body:
Put a rectangle on squared paper and count the little squares it covers. That count is its AREA — how much flat space the shape takes up.
Because we count in squares, area is measured in SQUARE units: square centimetres, written cm². One cm² is a square one centimetre along each side, about the size of your little fingernail.
Any shape has an area, however wiggly — it is always just the number of unit squares that fit inside.
sections.example: A rectangle covering 12 little centimetre squares has an area of 12 cm².

sections.heading: The rectangle shortcut: length × width
sections.body:
You do not have to count every square. A rectangle 9 cm long and 6 cm wide has 6 rows of 9 squares — and 6 rows of 9 is a multiplication: 9 × 6 = 54. Its area is 54 cm².
That is all the formula is: area of a rectangle = length × width, because the squares inside sit in equal rows. You are not learning a magic rule — you are counting squares the fast way.
sections.example: A rectangle 7 cm long and 4 cm wide: 7 × 4 = 28, so its area is 28 cm².

sections.heading: Perimeter is the distance around
sections.body:
Now imagine an ant walking right around the edge of the shape, back to where it started. The distance it walks is the PERIMETER.
Perimeter is a length, so it is measured in plain centimetres or metres — no little ² — because the ant walks a line, not a space.
To find it, add up ALL the sides. Every side, all the way round, missing none. For a rectangle that is two lengths and two widths.
sections.example: A rectangle 9 cm long and 6 cm wide: the ant walks 9 + 6 + 9 + 6 = 30 cm.

sections.heading: The perimeter shortcut for rectangles
sections.body:
A rectangle's opposite sides are equal, so instead of adding four numbers you can add the length and width once, then double it.
For a rectangle 7 cm long and 4 cm wide: 7 + 4 = 11, and double 11 is 22. Perimeter: 22 cm. Same answer as 7 + 4 + 7 + 4, with half the writing.
A square is even friendlier — all four sides equal, so its perimeter is one side times 4, and its area is one side times itself.
sections.example: A square with 5 cm sides: perimeter 5 × 4 = 20 cm, area 5 × 5 = 25 cm².

sections.heading: Which one does the question want?
sections.body:
Area and perimeter live on the same shape, so questions love to swap them — and the way to stay safe is to picture what is being done.
Painting a wall, covering a floor, laying a carpet? That fills the SPACE INSIDE — area. Building a fence, putting a border round a picture, walking the edge of a field? That travels AROUND — perimeter.
Before reaching for a formula, ask one question: is this about the inside, or the way round?
sections.example: A fence around a garden is perimeter. The grass seed to cover the garden is area.

mistakes.wrong: Finding the perimeter of a 9 by 6 rectangle as 9 + 6 = 15.
mistakes.right: The ant walks FOUR sides: 9 + 6 + 9 + 6 = 30 cm.
mistakes.why: One length and one width is only half the journey — double it, or add all four sides.

mistakes.wrong: Writing an area as 54 cm instead of 54 cm².
mistakes.right: Area counts squares, so its unit is square centimetres: 54 cm².
mistakes.why: cm measures a line; cm² measures space. The little ² says squares were counted.

mistakes.wrong: Working out fencing for a garden using length × width.
mistakes.right: A fence goes AROUND — that is perimeter, so add the sides.
mistakes.why: Length × width fills the inside. Ask first: inside, or the way round?

check.question: What does AREA measure?
check.explanation: Area is the count of unit squares that fit inside — the flat space the shape covers.

check.question: What is the area, in square centimetres, of a rectangle 9 cm long and 6 cm wide?
What is the perimeter, in centimetres, of a rectangle 9 cm long and 6 cm wide?
check.explanation: All four sides: 9 + 6 + 9 + 6 = 30 cm — or double 9 + 6.

check.question: Which unit is used for AREA?
check.explanation: Area counts squares, so its unit is the square centimetre.

check.question: What is the area, in square centimetres, of a rectangle 7 cm long and 4 cm wide?
What is the perimeter, in centimetres, of a rectangle 7 cm long and 4 cm wide?
A square has sides of 5 cm. What is its perimeter?
A square has sides of 5 cm. What is its area?
check.explanation: 5 × 5 = 25 cm² — a square's area is one side times itself.

check.question: A shape covers exactly 12 centimetre squares on squared paper. What is its area?
check.explanation: Area IS the count of unit squares — 12 squares means 12 cm².

check.question: Which of these is a PERIMETER question?
options: How much fence goes around the garden?
How much carpet covers the floor?
How much paint covers the wall?
How much grass seed covers the field?
check.answer: How much fence goes around the garden?
check.explanation: A fence travels around the edge — that is the perimeter. The other three fill a space, which is area.

practice.hint: Add all four sides — or double 6 + 3.
